Cubers have ~~tenths~~ ~~teens~~ ~~teeth~~ tens, sometimes hundreds of what we call *algorithms* memorized: Pre-defined move sequences intended to take the cube from one state to another but only moving specific pieces towards their desired spots while all the others are kept in place. With muscle memory and quick reflexes, often combined with the ability to "predict" how the cube will turn out after a specific sequence of moves, one is able to solve the cube in a matter of seconds. That's not to say every solve is pretty much the same - each solve is unique, since there's *43 quintillion* possible permutations for a cube: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubik%27s_Cube#cite_note-Vaughen-27 Also, here's the current Top 100 lowest times for solving a 3x3: https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/results/events.php?eventId=333&amp;regionId=&amp;years=&amp;show=100%2BPersons&amp;single=Single

Oh, I suspected this, actually. So, with that method you can't do a sighted solve without memorizing first because you may run into two issues: Parity and Special Targets. With that method, the four targets on the slice abide to a special rule: If they come second in a letter pair, you must to the inverse algorithm instead of the regular one (i.e.: BU instead of UB, DB instead of BD). This happens because the first letter of this pair (whichever it is) will offset the slice by 2, and then those pieces are positioned inverse to one another. Doing the inverse algorithm at the second letter of this pair will fix that, and the slice will end up fixed.  What I did when learning that method was writing down the memo and then doing a sighted solve following it to see how the cube would end up affected after each letter. If at the end you don't end up with a solved cube, you will be able to backtrack what you missed. Also, I suggest using scrambles for this. You won't run into Parity but the special cases might show up.

For perspective: While it is a fact that a professionally set up and maintained high-end instrument would allow me to become an objectively better player faster than my trusty ol' standard instrument ever could, I won't catch up to a virtuoso unless I earn my keep through extensive practice. Short answer: Loads of work. The good news is that you can learn it at your own pace and progressively switch into it from OP. Sorta like going from one advanced method to another - As you learn new algs you apply them if the case shows up. And when they do, the difference is mind-blowing. Also, while it is indeed a massive amount of algorithms, IMO it is not as hard as it sounds because they're far more intuitive than say, OLLs. While you can (and should) understand what an OLL/PLL does in terms of moving pieces around, taking F2L pairs and putting them back etcetera (which is a lot of stuff going on)... In 3Style you pretty much need to know how just 3 pieces are moving around. Takes a bit of getting used to, but once you do it makes it much easier to memorize the algs and better yet, understand what they do and how. Also, the more you learn the easier it gets because you're able to improvise a lot in cases you don't have a proper alg for yet. The simplest setup moves make it possible for you to apply what's basically the same algorithm to a whole different case (or cases) without even thinking. And again, the more sticker sets you learn, the more you're able to improvise and the easier it is to do so. I highly recommend you start transitioning into 3Style once you average below a certain threshold. I'm still far from knowing the full thing, but the little that I do already pushed me to break a significant barrier. It's a great investment and definitely not so hard - just takes lots of effort.

For 3Style algs, pretty much only execution. When I get comfortable with it, however, I'll do a few slow repeats just to track the pieces as they move around, as a way to understand  and also visualize what the algorithm does.  This IMO is an important step in learning algs because if I mess up during a solve, it is easier to backtrack and also if I happen to forget how to do it, I can improvise quickly from a different alg. For example, let's say I forgot how to do the alg for the DF-RU-DL cycle. Instead of panicking and resorting to the much slower solution, I would simply do an U2 setup into the alg for DF-LU-DL (which just so happens to be ridiculously fast as well, so if my think-ahead is on point, the loss in actual execution time is of less than 1 second).
